seo.title: Sliding Window — Stop Rebuilding What You Already Counted
altTitles: Sliding Window Explained Until It Sticks (DSA Pattern 2)
The Pattern Behind Every Subarray Question
seo.hook: A billion operations, or six thousand. Same houses.
seo.breakdown: the sliding window pattern, traced line by line, with the signal words that give it away

chapters.title: The words that give it away
The four problems to go and do

queries: maximum sum subarray of size k

scenes.narration: A row of houses, each with a number on the door. One question about them: a billion steps, or six thousand?
Pattern two of ten in the NBX Studio Dojo: Sliding Window. This is the one that turns a nested loop into a single pass, by refusing to count anything twice.

Same drill as last time: the question tells you the pattern if you read it properly. Watch for subarray, or substring, both meaning a run of items that sit next to each other. Watch for contiguous, which is the formal way of saying the same thing. And a size or a limit, which means either a fixed k or a rule the window must keep obeying. If the items don't have to be adjacent, this is not your pattern, and you're probably looking at a hash map or dynamic programming instead. Contiguous is the word to watch for, because it is doing more work than it looks like.

dsaSignals.caption: signals in the question

cells.sub: the same thing, in a string

cells.label: of size k

scenes.narration: Here's the obvious version. Stop at every position and add up the whole window from scratch. With six houses and a window of three that's twelve additions, which is nothing. But a million houses with a window of a thousand is a billion additions, and that program does not finish while anybody is watching. The sliding version does twelve for the small case too, and two million for the big one. The difference is what you refuse to redo.

dsaCost.headline: Why [recounting] hurts
dsaCost.caption: the same houses, two costs
dsaCost.premise: The same job priced two ways as the input grows: the obvious method against the pattern. Longer bar means more work.

scenes.narration: You're on a train, looking out of a window that shows exactly three houses at a time. Each house has a number painted on the door: how many cookies that house baked today. Two, one, five, one, three, two. You want the three houses in a row that baked the most between them. The slow way is to stop the train at every position and count all three houses again from nothing. It works, and on six houses you'd never feel it. On a million houses with a window of a thousand you would feel it, which is why the pattern exists.

dsaWindow.headline: A window onto [three houses]
dsaWindow.caption: the view from the train
dsaWindow.premise: You are on a train. Each box is a house you pass, and its number is how many cookies that house baked today. The window shows exactly k = 3 houses at once.

scenes.narration: Window sum equals sum of nums up to k. That colon-k slice means the first three houses, positions zero, one and two, so two plus one plus five is eight. And max sum starts as that same eight, because eight is the best score so far, for the very good reason that eight is the only score so far. Max sum is eight. Hold on to this moment, because it is the only time in the whole algorithm that we add a full window from scratch. Everything after this is repair work.

dsaWindow.headline: Count the first window [once]
dsaWindow.caption: the only full count
dsaWindow.premise: You are on a train. Each box is a house you pass, and its number is how many cookies that house baked today. The window shows exactly k = 3 houses at once.

lines.detail: Add up the first three houses. Once.
The best score so far is the only score so far.

scenes.narration: Now the train moves, and the loop starts at k rather than at zero, because the first k houses are already counted. Two things happen to your view, and only two. A new house comes in: house three, which baked one cookie, so we add it. And a house leaves: house zero, which baked two, so we subtract it. Eight plus one minus two is seven. Notice what we did not do. We never re-added houses one and two. They never left the window, so their cookies were never in question.

dsaWindow.headline: One in, [one out]
dsaWindow.caption: the train moves one house
dsaWindow.premise: You are on a train. Each box is a house you pass, and its number is how many cookies that house baked today. The window shows exactly k = 3 houses at once.

lines.detail: Start at k: the first window is already counted.
The house entering the view gets added.
The house leaving the view gets subtracted.

scenes.narration: Straight from the Dojo. The window total just dropped from eight to seven. Is seven the new best? Yes, seven is the new record. Or no, eight was better and we keep eight as the maximum. Have a think, and pause here if you'd like a moment. Ready? No. Seven is now; eight is the best ever seen, and the question asked for the best.

quiz.question: Window sum dropped 8 → 7. Is 7 the new best?
quiz.why: window_sum is now. max_sum is the best ever seen.

scenes.narration: That's what this line is for, and it's the line people skip. Max sum equals max of max sum and window sum. Window sum is the total you are looking at right now, and it goes up and down as the train moves. Max sum is the best total you have ever seen, and it only goes up. Two variables, two completely different jobs, and confusing them is the most common way to get this pattern wrong in an interview.

dsaWindow.headline: Two numbers, [two jobs]
dsaWindow.caption: now versus best
dsaWindow.premise: You are on a train. Each box is a house you pass, and its number is how many cookies that house baked today. The window shows exactly k = 3 houses at once.

lines.detail: Keep whichever is bigger: the record, or right now.

scenes.narration: Off it goes again. House four comes in with three cookies, house one leaves with one. Seven plus three minus one is nine, and nine beats our old record of eight. So max of eight and nine is nine, and the record moves. Two arithmetic operations for a window of three. And here is the part that matters: that would still be two operations for a window of a thousand, because the repair work has nothing to do with how big the window is.

dsaWindow.headline: A [new record]
dsaWindow.caption: nine beats eight
dsaWindow.premise: You are on a train. Each box is a house you pass, and its number is how many cookies that house baked today. The window shows exactly k = 3 houses at once.

lines.detail: Add the house that entered: plus three.

scenes.narration: Last stop. House five comes in with two, house two leaves with five, so nine plus two minus five is six, which is not a record, so max sum stays where it is. And we return nine. Every possible window of three has now been checked, and the winner was houses two, three and four. One pass down the street, two operations per step, and not one house counted twice.

dsaWindow.headline: Last stop, [and done]
dsaWindow.caption: one pass, finished
dsaWindow.premise: You are on a train. Each box is a house you pass, and its number is how many cookies that house baked today. The window shows exactly k = 3 houses at once.

lines.detail: Hand back the best window we ever saw.

scenes.narration: One more thing, because sliding window arrives in two shapes and interviewers use both. The fixed window is the one we just wrote, where the size never changes and the window simply slides. The variable window is different. It grows from the right until some rule breaks, then shrinks from the left until the rule holds again. Longest substring without repeating characters is the classic: grow until you hit a repeat, then pull the left edge past it. Same idea, same refusal to recount. Fixed size, you slide. Stated rule, you grow and shrink.

dsaSignals.headline: Fixed window, or [variable]
dsaSignals.caption: the two shapes it comes in
dsaSignals.premise: Words lifted straight out of the question, and the pattern each one points at. Red means the signal rules this pattern OUT.

cells.sub: size never changes, it just slides

cells.label: longest substring

cells.label: same refusal

scenes.narration: Four to go and do, and I'd do them in this order. Maximum Average Subarray is the fixed window you just wrote, almost line for line. Longest Substring Without Repeating is your first variable window. Permutation in String adds a frequency count inside the window. And Minimum Window Substring is the hard one that ties it all together.

data.heading: Do these four, in this order

scenes.narration: Three things to take with you. The signal is contiguous, a run of neighbours rather than any old selection. The move is to repair the total instead of rebuilding it, one in and one out. And keep two variables apart: the window you're in, and the best you've seen.
Next in the Dojo is Binary Search, where instead of sliding a window across the data we throw half of it away on every single step. Go and do Maximum Average Subarray first.
